title: U.S. Ends Duration of Status for Student Visas: What Employers Need to Know
excerpt: A new DHS rule replaces open-ended stays with fixed four-year admission periods for F-1, J-1, and I visa holders, creating new compliance burdens for employers before the September 15 deadline.
body:
• The DHS final rule, published July 17, eliminates "duration of status" for F-1 students, J-1 exchange visitors, and I visa holders, replacing it with fixed admission periods capped at four years — effective September 15, 2026.
  • Employers must now track Form I-94 expiration dates alongside program end dates and EADs, and should prepare for USCIS extension filings that carry fees, delays, and denial risk.
  • The post-completion grace period for F-1 students drops from 60 days to 30, compressing the window for OPT transitions and employer onboarding.
  • A Brookings-commissioned study estimates the rule could cost the U.S. economy $72–145 billion annually over ten years, with roughly half of surveyed international Ph.D. students saying they would not have come to the U.S. had the rule been in place.

The End of Duration of Status

On July 17, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security published a final rule that dismantles one of the longest-standing frameworks in U.S. immigration law. For nearly five decades, international students on F-1 visas, exchange visitors on J-1 visas, and foreign media representatives on I visas were admitted for "duration of status" — meaning they could remain in the country as long as they were enrolled in or complying with their authorized programs, without a fixed departure date on their paperwork.

That system ends on September 15, 2026. In its place, DHS is imposing fixed admission periods — generally capped at four years — stamped directly on the Form I-94 arrival record, according to the final rule published in the Federal Register. Anyone needing more time will have to file a formal extension application with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), a process that involves filing fees, biometrics, security checks, and the real possibility of denial.

What Changes for Employers

The practical implications for U.S. employers are substantial. As immigration attorney Bernard Wolfsdorf outlined in a detailed 25-point employer guide, companies will need to track a matrix of immigration dates that previously required little active management: Form I-94 expirations, Form I-20 or DS-2019 program end dates, employment authorization document (EAD) expiration dates, and extension filing and approval timelines.

"Fixed dates will drive immigration risk."

— Bernard Wolfsdorf, WR Immigration

Travel creates an additional wrinkle. A current D/S holder who leaves the country and reenters after September 15 will be placed into the new fixed-date system, regardless of when they were originally admitted. Employers should collect updated Forms I-94 from returning employees after every international trip.

The rule also cuts the post-graduation grace period for F-1 students from 60 to 30 days — a change that compresses the already tight window for transitioning from Optional Practical Training (OPT) to employer-sponsored status. Wolfsdorf warns that employers should update offer letters to avoid suggesting that work authorization or extension approval is guaranteed.

The Scale of the Problem

DHS itself estimates the rule will generate more than 400,000 additional USCIS applications per year — roughly evenly split between F-1 and J-1 categories. According to the Association of American Universities, that represents a 163% increase in this application type, hitting an agency already carrying a backlog of over 11.3 million cases and processing times that regularly exceed six months.

While a timely-filed extension allows the applicant to remain in the U.S. for up to 240 days while the case is pending, it does not automatically authorize continued employment, according to the Brookings Institution. That means processing delays could directly interrupt work, research, training, and onboarding — a reality that employers in healthcare, technology, and academia will feel most acutely.

The economic stakes are significant. A study commissioned by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine estimates the rule could reduce U.S. economic output by $72 to $145 billion annually over a decade. The analysis, conducted by researchers including Johns Hopkins economist Michael Clemens, surveyed roughly 1,000 international Ph.D. students and postdoctoral fellows at U.S. universities. About half said they either "definitely" or "probably" would not have come to the U.S. if the rule had been in place.

The Indian Diaspora at the Center

India sends the largest number of international students to the United States — approximately 330,000 during the 2023-24 academic year, according to India's Ministry of External Affairs. The new rule has triggered sharp concern in New Delhi. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal confirmed that India is in active communication with Washington to minimize difficulties for Indian students and travelers.

"As and when there are issues of difficulties, which are brought to our attention, in regard to genuine travellers and students... we take up those issues with the US side so as to minimise the difficulties that our people face."

— Randhir Jaiswal, MEA spokesperson

The rule hits particularly hard for doctoral students and medical trainees — fields where Indian nationals are heavily represented. More than 50% of first-time bachelor's recipients need more than four years to graduate, and the median doctoral student spends nearly six years on a dissertation. The International Medical Graduate Taskforce stated it would be "impossible" for physicians to complete many critical training programs within the four-year window, including general surgery, geriatrics, and cardiology residencies.

What Employers Should Do Now

With less than two months before the September 15 effective date, Wolfsdorf recommends employers take immediate steps: identify all employees and program participants in F, J, and I status; distinguish current D/S holders from those who will enter the fixed-date system; track all relevant immigration documents; flag individuals likely to require extensions; update onboarding and reverification procedures; and coordinate closely with university international offices and immigration counsel.

The rule could still face legal challenges or congressional review — DHS attempted a similar policy in 2018 that was blocked by a federal court, and a bipartisan group of four congressional representatives has urged the department to delay implementation. But employers cannot afford to wait for those outcomes. As Wolfsdorf notes, this is "one of the most significant changes to the international student and exchange-visitor system in decades," and the compliance clock is already ticking.
